title: Ironwood Systems — Private Network Security Deep-dive
topics: Audit logs & log retention for on-prem control plane
KMS key custody and rotation (HSM vs cloud KMS)
Network isolation, ingress/egress proxies, firewalling and deny-by-default architecture
summary: Redwood AE/SE ran a focused technical session with Ironwood's security and platform leads to validate private/VPC deployment controls. Discussed SOC 2 evidence mapping, RBAC/SSO integration patterns, audit log forwarding options, and detailed network isolation patterns including egress proxies, firewall zoning, and airgap considerations. Agreement to run a short benchmark and supply architecture diagrams, SOC 2 whitepaper, and a KMS integration checklist.
action_items: Maya Chen - Share SOC 2 evidence matrix + private deploy checklist - due 2027-03-05
Daniel Ortiz - Produce network diagram showing control plane/data plane egress paths and suggested firewall rules - due 2027-03-08
Priya Patel - Provide current infra CIDR ranges and list of allowed SaaS endpoints for egress allowlist - due 2027-03-04
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC2+ISO artifacts and deployment runbook link
Schedule in-person lab 2-hour bench on 2027-03-15 to validate egress proxy and KMS handshake
Customer to open temporary access ticket for Redwood SE to view private VPC peering config (read-only)
transcript:
Header: 2027-03-02 16:30 UTC | Duration: ~63m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Alice Park (CTO - Ironwood), Omar Reyes (Head of Security - Ironwood), Priya Patel (Platform/DevOps - Ironwood)
Links shared: https://redwood.internal/soc2-whitepaper (Redwood SOC2 summary), https://redwood.internal/private-deploy-runbook (deployment checklist), https://drive.ironwood/arch/diagram.pdf (customer network diagram reference)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, appreciate it. We're planning to go deep on the private deployment security posture — SOC 2 evidence mapping, RBAC/SSO, KMS and then the network isolation story. Does that agenda look good?
[00:15] Alice Park: Yep that sounds perfect. We're particularly nervous about egress controls and how audit trails will be produced for compliance.
[00:22] Daniel Ortiz: Great — we'll start with a quick recap of Redwood's private control plane model, then jump into the network flows. Just a heads up, I might pepper in some config samples.
[00:30] Omar Reyes: Awesome. Also, quick note: Ironwood intends to limit cloud KMS use for keys tied to PII; we may require HSM-backed KMS on-prem.
[00:40] Maya Chen: Noted. We have support for external KMS and HSMs in our Private product; Daniel will show the handshake and rotation flow.
[00:50] Priya Patel: And can we confirm SSO mapping? We use Okta and push groups via SCIM — need to ensure RBAC syncs and that role changes are auditable.
[01:05] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, we support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning; our RBAC model maps SAML groups to Redwood roles and we persist change events to the audit log. Small caveat: the provisioning sync is eventual — there can be a short window where a group change propagates.
[01:20] Alice Park: How short? Minutes? Hours? That affects our process for deprovisioning contractors.
[01:26] Daniel Ortiz: Typically under a minute for most deployments, worst case a couple minutes under heavy load. We'll add a recommended checklist to accelerate deprovisioning (force sync API).
[01:40] Omar Reyes: Okay. What about audit log retention; SOC 2 wants 12 months at least for certain events. Can Redwood private ship logs to our ELK/Splunk?
[01:50] Maya Chen: Yes — we have multiple export options: direct syslog, Kafka, S3-compatible sinks with KMS encryption, or push to SIEM via HTTPS. There's also a hosted-forwarder that can run in your VPC (no outbound to Redwood).
[02:05] Priya Patel: If we use the hosted-forwarder, does it still touch Redwood control plane? We're trying to minimize any egress to external accounts.
[02:10] Daniel Ortiz: The forwarder runs as a customer-managed service in your VPC and writes to your storage; it only calls your SIEM endpoints. Control plane calls are optional — for metrics we use safe-scrubbed telemetry, but logs can be fully customer-owned.
[02:25] Alice Park: Good. Let's dig into network isolation then — ingress and egress model.
[02:30] Daniel Ortiz: High level: we split into control plane and data plane. Control plane is optional to run in Redwood-managed SaaS or in a private control plane. Data plane runs in your VPC/on-prem via agents or a dedicated GPU pool. The key is deny-by-default egress from data plane with an egress proxy for required external calls (model downloads, telemetry if enabled).
[02:50] Omar Reyes: For model downloads — can we pre-stage model artifacts in our internal artifact store so the data plane never reaches out to external registries?
[02:58] Daniel Ortiz: Yes. You can import model binaries into an internal registry (S3, GCS, Artifactory). The runtime supports offline model mounting. We don't require any outbound to public container registries if you pre-provision.
[03:15] Priya Patel: How do we handle OS/patch updates for the runtime without outbound? We have a strict airgap process.
[03:22] Daniel Ortiz: For fully air-gapped setups we can do an offline image bundle; Redwood provides signed image tarballs and upgrade manifests you can pull into your private registry. It's a manual process but supported.
[03:35] Alice Park: Firewall rules — want specifics.
[03:38] Daniel Ortiz: Sure: recommend three zones: control-plane management, data-plane inference, and ops-only bastion/maintenance. Example rules: control-plane to data-plane mTLS port 8443 only, data-plane egress to internal artifact store over 443, egress proxy IPs for telemetry — everything else denied. We'll deliver a sample firewall policy.
[03:58] Omar Reyes: IPs — we need static egress endpoints. Can Redwood provide fixed IPs for the egress proxy?
[04:05] Maya Chen: For dedicated/private we can supply a static egress proxy endpoint that you host in your subnet; if you're using Redwood-managed egress we have a small egress range but for compliance you can host the proxy yourself to control IPs.
[04:20] Priya Patel: That helps. What about service accounts and key custody? We use centrally managed KMS with HSM for all encryption keys.
[04:29] Daniel Ortiz: Recommended approach: Redwood supports external KMS with envelope encryption. Customer KMS handles the root key; Redwood stores only encrypted data keys. You can configure automatic rotation and split keys via HSM. The control plane never has plaintext root keys.
[04:45] Omar Reyes: Can you show the key flow?
[04:48] Daniel Ortiz: (screen-share) Okay, slide — client writes request -> runtime generates data key -> data key encrypted with customer KMS (Encrypt API) -> encrypted payload stored. On decrypt, control plane calls KMS Decrypt only with IAM-supplied credentials. For on-prem HSMs we use an HSM gateway or KMIP adapter.
[05:10] Alice Park: I'm seeing some differences between your previous SOC 2 artifact and what I need for ISO 27001. Do you have mapping docs?
[05:18] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include a combined SOC 2 + ISO mapping for private deployments.
[05:24] Omar Reyes: Logging format — we need immutable log provenance and tamper-evidence for some artifacts. Can Redwood append an HMAC or sign logs with a key we manage?
[05:35] Daniel Ortiz: Currently we support signing logs at export time using a customer-provided key (HMAC). For stronger tamper-proof chains there is an option to push logs to an append-only ledger service you manage and we can write directly to it. We'll add an example.
[05:50] Priya Patel: About RBAC — do you support fine-grained runtime permissions like 'invoke-model-X' or is it per service?
[05:58] Daniel Ortiz: We support resource-level policies. You can create roles scoped to models, routes, and spaces. SCIM group -> role mapping can be as granular as you need.
[06:10] Alice Park: For SOC 2 we'll need evidence of access reviews. How does Redwood surface role membership change history?
[06:18] Maya Chen: All provisioning events are logged and there is an audit endpoint you can pull which contains timestamped events, actor, and the delta. We can export that to your compliance bucket on a schedule.
[06:30] Omar Reyes: Let's talk about egress whitelisting in practice — we have several internal SaaS endpoints (license manager, monitoring) that the runtime occasionally calls. We need to keep a tight allowlist.
[06:42] Daniel Ortiz: Best practice is to deploy an internal egress proxy inside your boundary that enforces an allowlist. Redwood's runtime supports configuring an HTTP transport that routes through your proxy — we can show sample envoy config.
[06:56] Priya Patel: Ok that sounds workable. Are there any parts that would still try to phone-home to Redwood?
[07:03] Maya Chen: Minimal. Health telemetry is optional. If you disable telemetry and host the control plane privately, there is no mandatory outbound. Some convenience features (auto-updates) can be toggled off.
[07:16] Alice Park: Can you also confirm data residency — data plane logs, and customer prompts must remain in-region.
[07:23] Daniel Ortiz: Yes — with private deployments data never leaves the configured region unless you opt-in to cross-region replication. We'll provide a configuration example.
[07:33] Omar Reyes: Let's try a hypothetical threat scenario: a compromised operator node on the data plane. What are compensating controls?
[07:42] Daniel Ortiz: Several: encrypted disks with keys in your KMS, process-level sandboxing, strict network segmentation to limit lateral movement, and runtime policy that requires signing of model binaries. We also recommend ephemeral workload identities with short-lived certs for inter-service auth.
[07:58] Maya Chen: Also worth adding: our telemetry will surface anomalous spikes in token volume, which can be alerted against. But you can route those alerts into your SIEM instead of Redwood.
[08:10] Priya Patel: Any latency impact from running egress through an internal proxy? If we put an Envoy between runtime and artifact store it adds hops.
[08:18] Daniel Ortiz: There's a measurable delta — usually single-digit milliseconds per request. For heavy download operations (model pulls) we recommend pre-staging and verifying checksums locally to avoid repeated remote calls.
[08:35] Alice Park: How do we validate that the control plane isn't accidentally leaking metadata? We need to prove minimum necessary data is shared.
[08:45] Daniel Ortiz: We have a data classification matrix. Control plane only receives metadata required for routing and operations unless you enable telemetry. We'll provide a data flow diagram and a list of fields we collect.
[08:58] Omar Reyes: Can Redwood's RBAC integrate with our least-privilege approval flow? We have an internal ticket system that triggers access elevation for specific tasks.
[09:08] Maya Chen: Yes — you can integrate via SCIM and a middleware that temporarily adds the SCIM group, or use a short-lived access token mechanism for admin tasks. We'll document both patterns.
[09:20] Priya Patel: Ok, on the practical side, what will Redwood need from us to start a pilot?
[09:26] Daniel Ortiz: Minimal: VPC CIDR ranges, the subnet where the data plane will run, a read-only list of current firewall rules, and KMS endpoint details (if you want to test key wraps). Also access to a staging bucket for logs.
[09:40] Alice Park: We'll gather those. Also interested in a short run where you attempt a SOC 2 evidence collection against our staging environment — like a smoke test for audit artifacts.
[09:50] Maya Chen: We can do that — we'll run a 2-hour evidence collection and produce a report.
[09:56] Omar Reyes: Anything about legal/contractual side? We have a mandatory subprocessor review and data processing addendum.
[10:03] Maya Chen: Our legal team has a standard DPA that includes subprocessor lists; we'll redline as needed. I'll include the DPA in the next email.
[10:12] Priya Patel: One more: key rotation windows. We require 90-day rotation for certain keys. Can Redwood support rotation without downtime?
[10:20] Daniel Ortiz: Yes — envelope key rotation is seamless: generate new data keys, rewrap, but we recommend a staged rotate with a canary host first. We'll share the rotation playbook.
[10:35] Alice Park: On monitoring and alerting — we'd like a catalogue of events that map to SOC 2 control failures. For example, failed login attempts > X, or SCIM provisioning failures flagged.
[10:48] Daniel Ortiz: We maintain a control-event map that maps internal events to common control IDs — we'll include that in the artifact pack.
[10:56] Omar Reyes: Are there any hard-blockers you see for our environment?
[11:00] Daniel Ortiz: Nothing fundamental — some operational effort for pre-staging models and configuring an internal egress proxy, and we recommend HSM integration for keys if you require it. All supported.
[11:12] Maya Chen: To wrap, we'll send the SOC2+ISO mapping, a sample firewall policy, the network diagram template, KMS integration checklist, and a proposed date for the 2-hour bench.
[11:24] Alice Park: Sounds good. Quick question from my side — can we get a signed statement about no plaintext PII leaving the VPC when telemetry is disabled?
[11:33] Maya Chen: We'll provide a letter that states default behavior and what needs to be disabled to guarantee that.
[11:40] Priya Patel: Great. Anything else?
[11:42] Omar Reyes: No, thanks. This was productive.
[11:45] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and the calendar invite for the bench.
---
Recap (auto): deliverables — SOC2+ISO mapping, firewall sample, network diagram, KMS checklist, schedule bench.
End of transcript.
